question: When AI companies pay for the books they learned from, how do we decide who should be paid?
reflection: Fair payment to the people whose work trained AI could make the technology a shared project instead of a quiet taking.

sources.subject: Meta AIRA3 beats 4,000 Kaggle teams, takes Gold at 8th place

one_line: AI labs are locking in huge computing budgets and building research agents, while the bills for training data and public patience come due.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly signs half a trillion dollars of compute
top_stories.what: An analysis by The Information estimates Anthropic agreed computing contracts worth about $517 billion in 11 months, far above figures it earlier shared with investors.
top_stories.why: Commitments this large show how much AI depends on power and data centres, which shapes where countries can compete.

top_stories.title: Authors and publishers dispute AI settlement money
top_stories.what: Anthropic's $1.5 billion copyright settlement could pay about $3,000 per book, but authors and publishers are filing competing claims where rights records are unclear.
top_stories.why: Clear records of who owns creative work will decide who benefits from AI licensing, a live issue for culture-sector bodies.

top_stories.title: Meta's research agent places in the top ten on Kaggle
top_stories.what: Meta's AIRA3, a group of agents sharing notes through a common forum, reportedly placed 8th of about 4,000 teams in a challenge to improve a model's reasoning.
top_stories.why: Agents that run experiments on their own could speed up applied research, but their findings will still need human review.

saudi_lens.text: No direct Saudi or regional link today.

idea.title: Rights registry readiness check
idea.pitch: Help a cultural body audit how well it records who owns each book, image or recording, so creators can claim AI licensing income.
idea.first_step: Sample fifty catalogue items and note how many have clear, current rights-holder records.

idea_kids.title: Whose story is it?
idea_kids.pitch: A classroom activity where children write and illustrate short stories, then practise giving credit when a friend borrows their ideas.
idea_kids.first_step: Prepare a simple credit card template with spaces for the story title, author and helper names.
